title: Consideration in Contract Law
text: Consideration is a fundamental requirement of a binding contract under English common law. In Currie v Misa [1875] LR 10 Ex 153, the court defined consideration as 'some right, interest, profit or benefit accruing to one party, or some forbearance, detriment, loss or responsibility given, suffered or undertaken by the other.' Past consideration is not good consideration as established in Roscorla v Thomas [1842] 3 QB 234. Consideration need not be adequate but must be sufficient — a peppercorn rent will suffice provided it has some value in the eyes of the law. Without consideration a promise is merely gratuitous and unenforceable unless made by deed under seal. The rule in Pinnel's Case [1602] 5 Co Rep 117a provides that payment of a lesser sum cannot be satisfaction for the whole, though promissory estoppel (Central London Property Trust v High Trees House [1947] KB 130) may prevent a party from going back on a clear and unambiguous promise not to enforce strict legal rights where the other party has relied on it.

title: Offer and Acceptance
text: A binding contract requires a clear offer and unequivocal acceptance. An offer must be distinguished from an invitation to treat (Fisher v Bell [1961] 1 QB 394 — display of goods is an invitation to treat, not an offer). Acceptance must mirror the offer exactly; any variation constitutes a counter-offer which destroys the original offer (Hyde v Wrench [1840] 3 Beav 334). A counter-offer must itself be accepted; mere enquiry does not destroy the original offer (Stevenson, Jacques & Co v McLean [1880] 5 QBD 346). Postal acceptance takes effect on posting (Adams v Lindsell [1818] 1 B & Ald 681), but communication of acceptance for instantaneous methods takes effect on receipt (Entores v Miles Far East [1955] 2 QB 327). Electronic acceptances under the Electronic Commerce (EC Directive) Regulations 2002 are deemed received when accessible to the offeror. An offer may be revoked at any time before acceptance provided revocation is communicated to the offeree (Byrne v Van Tienhoven [1880] 5 CPD 344).

title: Certainty of Terms
text: A contract will be void for uncertainty if essential terms are too vague to enforce. In Scammell v Ouston [1941] AC 251, the House of Lords held that an agreement 'on hire-purchase terms' was too uncertain to constitute a binding contract because there was no uniformly accepted meaning for those terms. Courts will, however, seek to uphold commercial agreements where possible by implying reasonable terms or construing language purposively using established trade custom or prior course of dealing. An agreement to agree on a material term in the future is not a binding contract (May and Butcher v R [1934] 2 KB 17). Where price is not fixed, courts may imply a reasonable price under the Sale of Goods Act 1979 s.8 in contracts for the sale of goods. The duty of good faith in negotiations does not generally exist in English law (Walford v Miles [1992] 2 AC 128), though specific agreements to negotiate in good faith may be enforceable in limited circumstances.

title: Breach of Contract and Remedies
text: A breach occurs when a party fails without lawful excuse to perform a contractual obligation. Remedies include: (1) Damages — aimed at putting the innocent party in the position they would have been in had the contract been performed (expectation loss: Robinson v Harman [1848] 1 Exch 850). Reliance loss and restitutionary damages are also available in appropriate cases. (2) Specific performance — available where damages are inadequate, typically for unique property or goods. (3) Injunction — to restrain threatened or continuing breach. (4) Rescission — available for misrepresentation, fraud, duress, or undue influence. The innocent party is under a duty to mitigate its loss (British Westinghouse v Underground Electric Rlys [1912] AC 673). Remoteness limits recovery to losses within the reasonable contemplation of the parties at contracting (Hadley v Baxendale [1854] 9 Exch 341; Victoria Laundry v Newman [1949] 2 KB 528). Consequential loss clauses in commercial contracts are common but subject to the reasonableness test under UCTA 1977.

title: Force Majeure and Frustration
text: Force majeure clauses excuse non-performance when a supervening event beyond the parties' control prevents or delays performance. Such clauses must be expressly included — there is no implied force majeure in English law. Strict construction applies: the event must fall squarely within the clause's language, and the party relying on it must typically give prompt notice. Where no force majeure clause exists, the doctrine of frustration may apply if a supervening event, not caused by either party and not foreseen at contracting, makes performance radically different from that contracted for (Davis Contractors Ltd v Fareham UDC [1956] AC 696). Financial hardship or increased cost alone does not frustrate a contract. The Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943 governs the restitutionary consequences: sums paid are recoverable; sums payable cease to be due; parties may retain or recover sums for valuable benefits conferred. COVID-19 pandemic cases clarified that government restrictions may engage force majeure but rarely frustration (Canary Wharf v EMA [2019]; Bank of New York Mellon v Cine-UK [2021]).

title: Non-Disclosure Agreements — Essential Elements
text: A valid non-disclosure agreement (NDA) must clearly identify the disclosing and receiving parties, define confidential information with sufficient precision, specify permitted uses and disclosure restrictions, state the duration of obligations, and include return or destruction provisions on termination. Under the equitable doctrine of breach of confidence established in Coco v AN Clark (Engineers) Ltd [1969] RPC 41, three requirements must be satisfied: the information must have the necessary quality of confidence (i.e. not be public knowledge), it must be imparted in circumstances importing an obligation of confidence, and there must be an unauthorised use causing detriment to the disclosing party. Information already in the public domain through no fault of the recipient cannot be protected. Standard NDAs include a mandatory notification clause requiring immediate written notice to the disclosing party's legal counsel upon discovery of any known or suspected breach. Mutual NDAs (MNDAs) impose reciprocal obligations; unilateral NDAs impose obligations only on the recipient. The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 (whistleblowing legislation) overrides NDA confidentiality where the disclosure relates to serious wrongdoing.

title: Injunctive Relief for Breach of Confidence
text: An injunction is the primary remedy for breach of confidence because damages are typically inadequate once confidential information has been disclosed to third parties. The applicant must satisfy the American Cyanamid balance of convenience test (American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd [1975] AC 396): (1) there is a serious question to be tried; (2) damages would not adequately compensate the claimant; (3) the balance of convenience favours granting the injunction. Springboard injunctions neutralise the competitive advantage wrongfully obtained from misuse of confidential information (Terrapin v Builders Supply [1967] RPC 375). Courts may grant injunctions on notice or, in urgent cases, without notice (ex parte / without notice applications) within 24–48 hours of a discovered breach. Any delay in applying weakens the claimant's case and may be treated as acquiescence. Search orders (Anton Piller orders) may be granted to preserve evidence. Account of profits or damages are available at trial. In employment contexts, post-termination confidentiality obligations must be distinguished from restraint of trade covenants, which are separately assessed for reasonableness.

title: Negligence — Elements and Caparo Test
text: The tort of negligence requires the claimant to establish four elements: (1) the defendant owed a duty of care; (2) the defendant breached that duty by falling below the standard of the reasonable person; (3) the breach caused the claimant's damage (factual causation: 'but for' test — Barnett v Chelsea & Kensington HMC [1969]); (4) the damage was not too remote (legal causation). The modern duty of care test from Caparo Industries plc v Dickman [1990] 2 AC 605 requires: (a) reasonable foreseeability of harm; (b) proximity of relationship; (c) that it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty. The standard of care is objective — what a reasonable person in the defendant's position would have done (Blyth v Birmingham Waterworks Co [1856] 11 Exch 781). Professionals are judged by the Bolam standard (Bolam v Friern HMC [1957] 1 WLR 582): a professional is not negligent if they acted in accordance with a responsible body of professional opinion. Contributory negligence under the Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945 apportions and reduces (but does not extinguish) the claimant's damages. Volenti non fit injuria (voluntary assumption of risk) may provide a complete defence.

title: Vicarious Liability
text: An employer is vicariously liable for torts committed by an employee in the course of employment without the employee needing to be personally at fault. The 'close connection' test (Lister v Hesley Hall Ltd [2001] UKHL 22) asks whether the tort was so closely connected with the employment that it would be fair and just to hold the employer liable. The Supreme Court in Various Claimants v Catholic Child Welfare Society [2012] UKSC 56 confirmed vicarious liability may extend beyond traditional employment relationships to 'relationships akin to employment'. Cox v Ministry of Justice [2016] UKSC 10 established a two-stage test: (1) whether the relationship is akin to employment; (2) whether the tort is closely connected to that relationship. Vicarious liability for independent contractors is generally not imposed unless the employer has assumed a non-delegable duty of care. The policy rationale is that employers are best placed to bear and distribute the risk of accidents caused by their enterprise activity.

title: Copyright — Subsistence and Infringement
text: Copyright subsists automatically in original literary, dramatic, musical, and artistic works under the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 (CDPA 1988). No registration is required in the UK. Originality requires that the work be the author's own intellectual creation (Infopaq International v Danske Dagblades Forening [2009] ECJ). The author is the first owner unless the work is created in the course of employment, in which case the employer is the first owner (s.11 CDPA 1988). Duration is generally life of author plus 70 years. Primary infringement (s.16–21) includes copying, issuing copies to the public, communicating to the public, and making adaptations, each requiring a causal link between the defendant's act and the protected work. Substantiality is judged qualitatively (Designers Guild v Russell Williams [2000] 1 WLR 2416). Defences include fair dealing for research, private study, criticism, review, and news reporting (ss.29–30 CDPA 1988). Secondary infringement requires knowledge or reason to believe the article is an infringing copy. Moral rights (integrity, attribution) are non-assignable but may be waived.

title: Trade Marks — Registration and Infringement
text: A trade mark is any sign capable of distinguishing goods or services of one undertaking from those of others. Registered marks under the Trade Marks Act 1994 confer exclusive rights to use the mark in relation to registered goods and services. Infringement under s.10 TMA 1994 occurs in three scenarios: (1) identical sign for identical goods/services (double identity — no confusion required); (2) similar sign for similar goods causing likelihood of confusion; (3) any sign taking unfair advantage of or causing detriment to a mark with a reputation in the UK. The EUIPO or UK IPO maintain registers; post-Brexit, EU trade marks no longer cover the UK. Passing off protects unregistered marks where goodwill, misrepresentation, and resulting damage can be proved (the 'trinity': Reckitt & Colman v Borden [1990] 1 WLR 491). Defences include descriptive use, comparative advertising (s.10(6) TMA), and exhaustion of rights for goods placed on the EEA market by the proprietor. Trade mark licences must be recorded at the registry to be effective against third parties. Revocation may be sought for five years of non-use or loss of distinctive character.

title: Patents — Grant, Validity and Infringement
text: A patent under the Patents Act 1977 grants a 20-year monopoly to exploit an invention in return for full public disclosure. To be patentable the invention must: (1) be novel (not form part of the state of the art at the priority date); (2) involve an inventive step (not be obvious to a person skilled in the relevant art); (3) be capable of industrial application; and (4) not fall within an excluded category (s.1(2) PA 1977), such as a discovery, mental act, or computer program as such. Infringement under s.60 PA 1977 includes making, disposing of, offering to dispose of, using, importing, or keeping a product embodying the patented claim, or performing a patented process. The doctrine of equivalents (Actavis UK Ltd v Eli Lilly [2017] UKSC 48) extends claim scope to variants that perform substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result, unless the patentee intentionally excluded the variant. Invalidity may be challenged by way of defence in infringement proceedings or by separate revocation proceedings at the UK IPO or Patents Court. Employee inventors may be entitled to a share of outstanding benefit under ss.39–43 PA 1977.

title: Unfair Dismissal — Rights and Procedure
text: Employees with two years' continuous employment have the right not to be unfairly dismissed under the Employment Rights Act 1996 (ERA 1996). The employer must establish one of five potentially fair reasons for dismissal: (1) capability or qualifications; (2) conduct; (3) redundancy; (4) statutory bar to continued employment; (5) some other substantial reason (SOSR) (s.98 ERA 1996). Even with a fair reason, the dismissal must be carried out by means of a fair procedure. The ACAS Code of Practice on Disciplinary and Grievance Procedures is not legally binding but Employment Tribunals must take it into account; failure to follow it can increase any compensatory award by up to 25%. The basic award is calculated by reference to age, weekly pay (capped), and length of service. The compensatory award is subject to a statutory cap (currently £115,115 or 52 weeks' pay, whichever is lower). Claims must be brought to the Employment Tribunal within three months less one day from the effective date of termination, following mandatory ACAS Early Conciliation. Automatically unfair dismissals (e.g. for whistleblowing, pregnancy, or trade union activities) do not require the qualifying service period.

title: Equality Act 2010 — Protected Characteristics and Claims
text: The Equality Act 2010 consolidates and extends protection against discrimination in employment across nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation. Direct discrimination involves treating a person less favourably because of a protected characteristic than a real or hypothetical comparator (s.13 EA 2010). Indirect discrimination arises when a provision, criterion or practice (PCP) that appears neutral places persons sharing a protected characteristic at a particular disadvantage that cannot be justified as a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim (s.19 EA 2010). Harassment is unwanted conduct related to a protected characteristic that has the purpose or effect of violating dignity or creating an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating or offensive environment (s.26 EA 2010). Victimisation protects those who carry out a protected act (s.27 EA 2010). Disability discrimination additionally requires reasonable adjustments (s.20 EA 2010). ET claims must be brought within three months less one day of the discriminatory act, following ACAS Early Conciliation. There is no cap on compensation for discrimination claims; injury to feelings awards are assessed using the Vento bands.

title: Notice Periods, Garden Leave and Wrongful Dismissal
text: At common law every employment contract contains an implied term of reasonable notice. The Employment Rights Act 1996 s.86 provides statutory minimum notice periods: one week per completed year of service up to a maximum of twelve weeks. Contractual notice periods often exceed statutory minima. Wrongful dismissal is a common law breach of contract claim available from day one of employment, without the two-year qualifying period required for unfair dismissal. It arises when the employer dismisses without giving due notice (or payment in lieu) without lawful justification (e.g. gross misconduct). Damages are limited to the remuneration payable during the notice period; future career losses are not recoverable. Garden leave clauses allow the employer to keep the employee away from the workplace while they remain employed and paid, serving to protect confidential information and client relationships. Payment in lieu of notice (PILON) clauses allow immediate termination on payment of notice period salary. Summary dismissal without notice is permitted only for gross misconduct sufficient to repudiate the contract. An employee who accepts a repudiatory breach by the employer may claim constructive dismissal.

title: Sale of Land — Formalities and Completion
text: Contracts for the sale or other disposition of an interest in land must comply with the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989 s.2: they must be made in writing, signed by or on behalf of each party, and incorporate all expressly agreed terms in one document or by reference. Non-compliance renders the contract void (not merely voidable). The equitable doctrine of proprietary estoppel may provide a remedy where strict formality requirements would produce an unconscionable result (Cobbe v Yeoman's Row [2008] UKHL 55; Thorner v Major [2009] UKHL 18). The sale process proceeds in stages: pre-contract searches and enquiries, exchange of contracts (which creates a binding obligation), requisitions on title, and completion. Completion transfers the legal estate by deed (Law of Property Act 1925 ss.52, 205(1)(ii)). Registration of title at HM Land Registry is required to transfer the legal estate in registered land (Land Registration Act 2002 s.27). Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT) is payable on completion; returns must be filed within 14 days.

title: Leasehold — Essential Elements and Statutory Protections
text: A lease requires three certainties established in Street v Mountford [1985] AC 809: a certain term, exclusive possession, and rent (though rent is no longer strictly essential following Ashburn Anstalt v Arnold [1989] Ch 1). The label attached by the parties is not determinative; courts look to the substance of the arrangement. A lease of more than three years must be granted by deed (Law of Property Act 1925 s.52) except for short leases taking effect in possession at market rent (s.54(2)). Leases must be distinguished from licences, as only a lease creates a property right binding on third parties. Commercial tenants are entitled to lease renewal under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954 unless the landlord successfully opposes on specified grounds. Residential tenants benefit from the Protection from Eviction Act 1977 (prohibition on harassment and illegal eviction) and the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 s.11 (implied repairing obligation for short residential tenancies). Service charges in long residential leases are regulated under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 ss.18–30.

title: Limitation Periods — Key Time Limits under the Limitation Act 1980
text: The Limitation Act 1980 prescribes the periods within which civil proceedings must be commenced. Key periods: Contract — six years from breach (s.5); twelve years for specialty contracts (deeds) (s.8). Tort (general) — six years from when damage occurs (s.2). Personal injury — three years from the date of injury or from the claimant's date of knowledge, whichever is later (s.11); courts have a discretion to disapply (s.33). Latent damage in negligence — six years from damage, or three years from knowledge of damage and its attributable cause, subject to a 15-year long-stop (ss.14A–14B). Defamation — one year (Defamation Act 1996 s.5). Fraud, deliberate concealment, or mistake postpones the limitation period until the claimant could with reasonable diligence have discovered the relevant facts (s.32). Proceedings are 'brought' on the date the claim form is issued by the court. Limitation is a procedural defence that must be pleaded; it does not extinguish the underlying right. In construction disputes, section 1 of the Latent Damage Act 1986 provides additional protection.

title: UK GDPR — Key Principles, Lawful Bases, and Data Subject Rights
text: The UK GDPR (retained post-Brexit in the UK GDPR 2018) and the Data Protection Act 2018 regulate the processing of personal data of individuals in the UK. Six lawful bases for processing personal data (Article 6 UK GDPR): consent, performance of a contract, compliance with a legal obligation, protection of vital interests, performance of a public task, and legitimate interests (subject to balancing test). Special category data (health, biometric, political opinions, etc.) requires an additional condition under Article 9 and Schedule 1 DPA 2018. The six data protection principles (Article 5): lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality. Data subjects have rights to: access (Subject Access Request — one month to respond), rectification, erasure ('right to be forgotten'), restriction, portability, and objection. Data breach notification to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) is required within 72 hours of discovery where the breach is likely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms. The ICO can impose fines up to £17.5 million or 4% of global annual turnover (whichever is higher) for serious violations.

title: Directors' Duties under the Companies Act 2006
text: The Companies Act 2006 ss.171–177 codifies seven general duties of directors owed to the company: (1) s.171 — act within powers (in accordance with the company's constitution and for proper purposes); (2) s.172 — promote the success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole, having regard to long-term consequences, employees, suppliers, community, and environment; (3) s.173 — exercise independent judgment; (4) s.174 — exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence (objective and subjective test); (5) s.175 — avoid conflicts of interest (especially in exploitation of property, information, or opportunity); (6) s.176 — not to accept benefits from third parties; (7) s.177 — declare interest in proposed transactions or arrangements. Breach of duty may give rise to an action by the company for account of profits, damages, or injunction. Derivative claims by shareholders may be brought under ss.260–264 CA 2006 with court permission. Shadow directors and de facto directors are subject to most of these duties. Directors of insolvent companies must consider creditors' interests (s.172(3) CA 2006; Sequana [2022] UKSC 25).

title: Dispute Resolution — Litigation, Arbitration and Mediation
text: Commercial disputes in England and Wales may be resolved through litigation, arbitration, mediation, or other ADR mechanisms. Litigation in the Business and Property Courts (including the Commercial Court, Chancery Division, and Technology and Construction Court) is governed by the Civil Procedure Rules 1998. The overriding objective is to deal with cases justly and at proportionate cost (CPR r.1.1). Parties are expected to comply with pre-action protocols and consider ADR before issuing proceedings; unreasonable refusal to mediate may result in adverse costs orders (Halsey v Milton Keynes General NHS Trust [2004] EWCA Civ 576). Arbitration under an arbitration clause is governed by the Arbitration Act 1996; the seat of arbitration determines the supervisory court. LCIA, ICC, UNCITRAL, and ad hoc arbitrations are common in international commercial disputes. Mediation is a confidential, without-prejudice process in which a neutral mediator assists parties to reach a negotiated settlement. Settlement agreements should be recorded in a written Tomlin Order (for court proceedings) or binding settlement agreement. Costs generally follow the event in litigation (CPR r.44.2); in arbitration, costs are at the tribunal's discretion.

title: Liquidated Damages and Penalty Clauses
text: A liquidated damages clause specifies in advance the sum payable on breach and is enforceable if it represents a genuine pre-estimate of loss at the time of contracting (Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Co v New Garage & Motor Co [1915] AC 79). A penalty clause — one that is extravagant, unconscionable, or not proportionate to any legitimate interest of the innocent party — will not be enforced; the innocent party is limited to proving actual loss. The Supreme Court in Cavendish Square Holding BV v Makdessi; ParkingEye Ltd v Beavis [2015] UKSC 67 reformulated the test: a clause is penal only if it imposes a detriment on the breaching party that is out of all proportion to any legitimate interest of the innocent party in enforcement. A clause protecting a legitimate business interest at a level that is not extravagant will be upheld even if it exceeds the likely financial loss. Forfeiture clauses in leases and deposits in land contracts are subject to equitable relief against forfeiture.

title: Corporate Insolvency — Key Processes and Directors' Exposure
text: UK corporate insolvency is governed by the Insolvency Act 1986 and the Corporate Insolvency and Governance Act 2020. Key processes: (1) Administration — collective procedure to rescue the company as a going concern, achieve a better result than winding up, or realise property for secured or preferential creditors. The administrator is an officer of the court with a duty to act in the interests of creditors as a whole. (2) Liquidation (winding up) — compulsory (court order) or voluntary (creditors' or members'). Assets are realised and distributed in statutory priority: fixed charge holders, liquidator's expenses, preferential creditors (employees' wages, pension contributions), floating charge holders, unsecured creditors, shareholders. (3) Company Voluntary Arrangement (CVA) — a compromise with creditors binding on all unsecured creditors if approved by 75% in value. (4) Restructuring Plan — court-sanctioned plan under CA 2006 s.901A enabling cross-class cram-down of dissenting creditors. Directors may face personal liability for wrongful trading (IA 1986 s.214 — continuing to trade when they knew or ought to have known there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation), fraudulent trading (s.213), and misfeasance. Disqualification proceedings may follow under the Company Directors Disqualification Act 1986.
